title: Anxiety, stress and wellbeing
introHtml:
Regular self-testing lowers exam anxiety, because it replaces vague worry with concrete evidence of what you know. Alongside that, a few habits keep stress at a level that helps rather than blocks.

Some stress is useful: it sharpens attention and gets you to the desk. The trouble starts when worry takes up the mental space you need for the work itself. Working memory, the small "desk" your mind thinks on, is shared between the task and the worry, so a head full of "what if I fail" has less room for the equation in front of it. The items below either shrink the worry, free up that desk, or keep your body (sleep, movement, food) in a state where learning can happen. A note on limits: these are self-help habits for everyday study stress, not treatment. If anxiety, low mood or exhaustion is lasting for weeks, affecting sleep, eating or daily life, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to a professional (see the last item).

items.title: Test yourself often, in low-stakes ways
items.leadHtml: Frequent practice makes the real exam feel familiar.

parts.why: Anxiety feeds on uncertainty. When you only re-read, you never find out whether you could answer under pressure, so the exam is a leap into the dark. Low-stakes quizzing turns the unknown into a known: you have already seen yourself retrieve the material many times. It is like a rehearsal before a concert; the stage is still scary, but it is a stage you have stood on. In a large classroom study, most middle and high school students said regular retrieval practice made them less nervous about tests.
parts.how:
1. Quiz yourself in every session with questions where nothing is at stake: flashcards, blank-page recall, a few past questions.
  2. Treat wrong answers as information ("I need to revisit X"), never as a verdict.
  3. In the last weeks, add one or two full practice papers under timed, exam-like conditions.

examples.simple: A school student does five quick questions on each chemistry topic at the start of each lesson-review, so the test feels like "just more of the same".
examples.nontrivial: A law student who freezes in oral exams asks a friend to quiz them out loud once a week. The content is the same as the written practice, but rehearsing the format (speaking, being watched) is what lowers the fear.
examples.html:
• Simple: A school student does five quick questions on each chemistry topic at the start of each lesson-review, so the test feels like "just more of the same".
  • Non-trivial: A law student who freezes in oral exams asks a friend to quiz them out loud once a week. The content is the same as the written practice, but rehearsing the format (speaking, being watched) is what lowers the fear.

parts.watch: If every practice set feels like a judgement on your worth, lower the stakes further: do it alone, ungraded, or with an open book for the first round.

reading.html: How can we reduce student anxiety?, RetrievalPractice.org

items.title: Worry dump
items.leadHtml: Spend 5 to 10 minutes writing down your worries before studying or before an exam. It frees up working memory.

parts.why: Worries behave like browser tabs left open: each one quietly uses some of your mental capacity, even when you are not looking at it. Writing them down closes some of the tabs. Once a worry is on paper, your mind no longer has to keep rehearsing it in case it gets forgotten. In a study published in Science, students who wrote freely about their test worries for 10 minutes before an exam did better than those who did not, and the benefit was largest for the most anxious students.
parts.how:
1. Before a session or exam, set a timer for 5 to 10 minutes.
  2. Write continuously about what you are worried about and how you feel. Spelling and logic do not matter; nobody will read it.
  3. Close the page (or throw it away) and start the first task straight away.

examples.simple: Before a maths test, a student writes "I always mess up fractions, I'm worried about running out of time" and then starts the paper feeling lighter.
examples.nontrivial: A doctoral student with a looming viva keeps a running "worry file". Each morning she adds to it for five minutes, then adds one concrete action next to each worry where an action exists ("ask supervisor about chapter 3 methods"). The writing empties the head; the action column stops the same worry returning tomorrow.

items.title: Define a stopping point
items.leadHtml: Anxious students often never feel "done". Decide in advance what a finished day looks like, and stop when you reach it.

parts.why: There is always more you could study, so "until I feel ready" never arrives. Without a finish line, the day ends with guilt instead of rest, and that guilt follows you into the evening. A pre-set target gives you a way to win the day. Research on unfinished goals also shows that making a concrete plan for what remains is enough to stop those goals intruding on your thoughts: the mind lets go once it trusts there is a plan.
parts.how:
1. In the morning (or the night before), write the day's finish line: "3 practice question sets, review cards, outline essay section 2".
  2. When it is done, write tomorrow's first task on a note. This is your "shutdown".
  3. Close the books and actually stop, even if you have energy left. Spare energy is tomorrow's head start.

examples.simple: A language learner's finished day is "today's flashcards plus one 15-minute conversation". After that, the evening is free.
examples.nontrivial: An engineering student in exam season sets a finish line by output, not hours ("two past papers marked and errors logged"). On a good day she is done by 4 pm and stops anyway; on a bad day she accepts finishing late rather than moving the line. The point is that the line is decided by the calm morning self, not the anxious evening self.

items.title: Productive struggle vs panic
items.leadHtml: Struggling to recall is normal and useful. Panic is a signal to pause, breathe and shrink the task.

parts.why: The effort of pulling an answer out of memory is exactly what strengthens it (a "desirable difficulty"), like the strain of a muscle during a workout. But there is a line: once stress floods your working memory, you stop thinking and start spinning. The skill is telling the two apart. Struggle feels like "it is on the tip of my tongue"; panic feels like "I can't do any of this".
parts.how:
1. When you get stuck, give yourself a short, fixed attempt (for example 1 to 2 minutes), then check the answer. That is productive struggle.
  2. If you notice racing thoughts, a tight chest or the urge to flee, stop. Do one minute of slow breathing (next item).
  3. Shrink the task until it feels doable again: one question instead of the whole set, one paragraph instead of the chapter.

examples.simple: A student blanks on a vocabulary word, gives it 30 seconds, checks, and moves on. That is struggle working as intended.
examples.nontrivial: A physics student facing a long, unfamiliar problem feels panic rising. Instead of staring at the whole thing, she writes down only what is given and what is asked. That small, certain step calms her enough to see which equation fits. Panic shrank because the task did.
examples.html:

  • Non-trivial: A physics student facing a long, unfamiliar problem feels panic rising. Instead of staring at the whole thing, she writes down only what is given and what is asked. That small, certain step calms her enough to see which equation fits. Panic shrank because the task did.

items.title: Breathing
items.leadHtml: A slow exhale, or two inhales through the nose and one long exhale (the physiological sigh), calms the body within a minute.

parts.why: Breathing is one of the few parts of the stress response you can control directly. Long, slow exhales nudge the nervous system towards its "rest" mode and slow the heart; the double inhale reopens the tiny air sacs in the lungs so the long exhale clears more carbon dioxide. Think of it as a manual brake for a body that has hit the accelerator. In a month-long randomised study, five minutes a day of "cyclic sighing" improved mood more than mindfulness meditation and lowered breathing rate.
parts.how:
1. Inhale through your nose until your lungs feel comfortably full.
  2. Take a second, shorter inhale on top to fill them completely.
  3. Breathe out slowly through your mouth until empty. Make the exhale longer than the inhales.
  4. Repeat 1 to 3 times for a quick reset, or for about 5 minutes as a daily practice.

examples.simple: Two physiological sighs in the waiting room before an oral exam or a driving test.
examples.nontrivial: A music student uses five minutes of cyclic sighing every morning during audition season, not just before performing. The daily practice makes the technique automatic, so it is available on the day instead of being one more new thing to remember under stress.
examples.html:
• Simple: Two physiological sighs in the waiting room before an oral exam or a driving test.
  • Non-trivial: A music student uses five minutes of cyclic sighing every morning during audition season, not just before performing. The daily practice makes the technique automatic, so it is available on the day instead of being one more new thing to remember under stress.

parts.time: Under a minute for a reset; 5 minutes for a daily practice.
parts.watch: If you feel dizzy, slow down and breathe normally. Breathing exercises help with everyday stress but are not a substitute for treatment of an anxiety disorder.

items.title: Reframe stress
items.leadHtml: Telling yourself that a racing heart is your body getting ready to perform helps more than trying to calm down.

parts.why: Anxiety and excitement feel almost the same in the body: fast heart, sweaty hands, alertness. What differs is the label. "I'm anxious, this is bad" turns the arousal into a threat signal; "my body is gearing up" turns it into fuel. Trying to force yourself calm often fails, because you are fighting a physical state. Relabelling works with it instead. In one study, students told before a practice exam that arousal can improve performance scored higher on the maths section, both in the lab and on the real exam later.
parts.how:
1. Notice the signs (heart, breath, stomach).
  2. Say to yourself, silently or on paper: "This is my body getting ready. Energy, not danger."
  3. Point the energy at the first concrete action: read question 1.

examples.simple: An athlete's pre-race nerves are the same as a student's pre-exam nerves; athletes simply learn to call them "readiness".
examples.nontrivial: A trainee lawyer before her first moot court feels her heart pounding. Instead of "calm down", she thinks "good, I'm switched on". She still feels the arousal, but it stops snowballing into "something is wrong with me", and she uses the alertness to listen sharply to the judge's questions.
examples.html:
• Simple: An athlete's pre-race nerves are the same as a student's pre-exam nerves; athletes simply learn to call them "readiness".
  • Non-trivial: A trainee lawyer before her first moot court feels her heart pounding. Instead of "calm down", she thinks "good, I'm switched on". She still feels the arousal, but it stops snowballing into "something is wrong with me", and she uses the alertness to listen sharply to the judge's questions.

parts.watch: Reframing works for normal performance stress. It is not meant to override signals that something is genuinely wrong, such as panic attacks or anxiety that lasts all day.

items.title: Self-compassion over perfectionism
items.leadHtml: Talk to yourself the way you would talk to a friend. A missed day is data, not a failure.

parts.why: Many students fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. The research points the other way. Harsh self-criticism makes failure feel threatening, so you avoid looking at your mistakes. Self-compassion makes failure safe enough to examine and fix. In experiments, students who were encouraged to be self-compassionate after failing a test spent more time studying for a retest than those who were simply given a self-esteem boost.
parts.how:
1. When you slip, notice the inner voice. Would you say that sentence to a friend?
  2. Rewrite it as you would for a friend: "That was a hard week. What got in the way, and what is one thing to change?"
  3. Log the slip as data in your planner ("missed Tuesday: too tired after work") and adjust the plan, not your self-worth.

examples.simple: After a bad quiz score a student writes "I didn't know the dates yet; I'll do 10 cards a day this week" instead of "I'm hopeless at history".
examples.nontrivial: A self-taught programmer who skipped two weeks of a course is tempted to restart from lesson one "to do it properly". With a kinder lens he sees that the urge to restart is perfectionism. He reviews quickly, picks up where he left off, and treats the gap as a lesson about scheduling during busy work weeks.

items.title: Compare less
items.leadHtml: Students in competitive programmes (medicine, law, engineering, music conservatoires, top schools) often compare hours, grades and resources. Track your own progress instead.

parts.why: We judge ourselves by comparison with others almost automatically; social psychologists have studied this since Leon Festinger's work in the 1950s. The problem is what we compare with. You see other people's highlight reel (the 12-hour library day, the top mark) and compare it with your own behind-the-scenes. Upward comparison with people who seem better often lowers mood and confidence, and hours studied is a poor measure anyway: one focused hour of self-testing can beat three hours of re-reading. Comparing yourself with your own past self is a fair race.
parts.how:
1. Keep a simple record of your own measures: practice scores, topics moved from "new" to "solid", cards reviewed.
  2. Once a week, compare with last week or last month, not with classmates.
  3. Mute or limit study-flex group chats and social media in exam season.
  4. Use others for ideas ("what resource do you like for this?"), not for verdicts.

examples.simple: A school student stops asking friends "how many hours did you do?" and instead notes her own weekly quiz percentage.
examples.nontrivial: A conservatoire violinist used to compare his practice hours with a classmate who practises six hours a day. Tracking his own recordings week by week showed his intonation improving steadily on three focused hours. He kept his schedule, and the comparison stopped costing him sleep.

items.title: Sleep 7 to 9 hours
items.leadHtml: Memory is consolidated during sleep. All-nighters lower exam performance.

parts.why: During sleep the brain replays what you learned during the day and moves it from short-term storage into longer-lasting memory. Think of the day as writing notes on a whiteboard and sleep as copying them into a notebook before the board is wiped. Skip the copying and much of the day is lost. Sleep also restores attention and mood, which you need in the exam itself. A study of university students who wore activity trackers through a semester found that sleep duration, quality and consistency together explained nearly a quarter of the differences in their grades.
parts.how:
1. Aim for 7 to 9 hours (teenagers often need more), at roughly the same times every day, including weekends.
  2. Protect sleep most in the week before exams, when it is most tempting to cut.
  3. If you must choose, sleep and review in the morning rather than stay up late.

examples.simple: A student who learned a set of new vocabulary in the evening remembers more of it the next morning than after the same number of hours awake.
examples.nontrivial: A history student facing two exams on consecutive days plans her "late night" for two days before, not the night between. The night before the first exam she sleeps normally so that the material is consolidated and she is sharp, and does a short morning recall session instead of a late cram.

• Simple: A student who learned a set of new vocabulary in the evening remembers more of it the next morning than after the same number of hours awake.
  • Non-trivial: A history student facing two exams on consecutive days plans her "late night" for two days before, not the night between. reading.html: Okano, K., Kaczmarzyk, J. R., Dave, N., Gabrieli, J. D. E. & Grossman, J. C. (2019). Sleep quality, duration, and consistency are associated with better academic performance in college students. npj Science of Learning.

items.bodyHtml:
Memory is consolidated during sleep. All-nighters lower exam performance.

Why it works. During sleep the brain replays what you learned during the day and moves it from short-term storage into longer-lasting memory. Think of the day as writing notes on a whiteboard and sleep as copying them into a notebook before the board is wiped. Skip the copying and much of the day is lost. Sleep also restores attention and mood, which you need in the exam itself. A study of university students who wore activity trackers through a semester found that sleep duration, quality and consistency together explained nearly a quarter of the differences in their grades.

How to do it.

  1. Aim for 7 to 9 hours (teenagers often need more), at roughly the same times every day, including weekends.
  2. Protect sleep most in the week before exams, when it is most tempting to cut.
  3. If you must choose, sleep and review in the morning rather than stay up late.

Examples.

  • Simple: A student who learned a set of new vocabulary in the evening remembers more of it the next morning than after the same number of hours awake.
  • Non-trivial: A history student facing two exams on consecutive days plans her "late night" for two days before, not the night between. The night before the first exam she sleeps normally so that the material is consolidated and she is sharp, and does a short morning recall session instead of a late cram.

Watch out. Ongoing trouble falling or staying asleep is worth raising with a doctor (GP) or your student health service.

items.title: Exercise
items.leadHtml: Even a 20-minute walk improves mood, focus and sleep.

parts.why: Movement increases blood flow to the brain and releases chemicals that support attention and the growth of new connections, especially in the hippocampus, a region central to memory. It also burns off some of the physical tension that stress builds up, a bit like letting steam out of a pressure cooker. You do not need a gym: regular moderate activity like brisk walking shows benefits.
parts.how:
1. Put movement in the plan like a class: a 20 to 30 minute walk, cycle, swim or session most days.
  2. Use it as a break between study blocks, not as a reward you only earn at the end.
  3. On exam days, a short walk before the exam can settle nerves.

examples.simple: A student walks to the library the long way, 20 minutes, and arrives more alert than after the bus.
examples.nontrivial: A self-taught coder who is stuck on a problem goes for a walk with the problem but without the screen. The movement lifts her mood, and the break gives her mind room to reorganise the problem, so she often comes back with the solution. Walking becomes both a wellbeing habit and a thinking tool.

items.title: Food, caffeine and screens
items.leadHtml: Regular meals, caffeine before early afternoon, and screens off before bed.

parts.why: Your brain runs on a steady supply of energy, so long gaps without food make concentration and mood dip. Caffeine blocks the chemical signal of sleepiness, but it lingers for many hours: in a sleep-lab study, a strong dose taken six hours before bed still cut sleep by more than an hour, and people did not notice the loss. So the afternoon coffee quietly steals from tonight's memory consolidation. Screens at night keep the mind switched on and push bedtime later.
parts.how:
1. Eat regular meals on study days; keep a simple snack and water at the desk.
  2. Set a caffeine cut-off around early afternoon (adjust to your bedtime: at least 6 hours before, more if you are sensitive).
  3. Put your phone away, out of reach, 30 to 60 minutes before bed; read paper or listen to something calm.

examples.simple: A student who used to have energy drinks at 6 pm switches to an earlier coffee and finds she falls asleep faster.
examples.nontrivial: A nurse studying part-time on shifts cannot use a clock-based cut-off. She uses "no caffeine in the last 6 hours before my planned sleep", whatever time that is, and keeps a fixed wind-down routine after night shifts. The rule adapts to her life instead of breaking on it.

items.title: Protected time off
items.leadHtml: At least one half-day per week without study. Rest is part of the plan.

parts.why: Recovery only happens when you actually switch off. Half-studying while feeling guilty is neither rest nor work. A protected block works like the rest days in an athlete's training plan: the gains come partly during the recovery, and athletes who skip it get injured. Planned time off also makes the study time more focused, because you know a break is coming and do not need to steal it.
parts.how:
1. Pick a fixed slot each week (for example Saturday afternoon) and write it in the planner as an appointment.
  2. Fill it with something that is not a screen version of studying: friends, sport, a hobby, nature.
  3. Keep it even in exam season, perhaps shorter. Cutting it to zero is usually what tips stress into burnout.

examples.simple: A school student keeps Sunday afternoon for football and does not open books, and finds Monday's session easier to start.
examples.nontrivial: A PhD student with no external schedule finds herself working a little every day and never feeling rested. She sets a hard rule: no work from Saturday 1 pm until Sunday evening, with the shutdown ritual from "Define a stopping point" on Saturday morning. Her weekly output stays the same, but the quality of her weekday focus improves.

items.title: Ask for help early
items.leadHtml: University counselling, a doctor (GP), or student wellbeing services. Burnout and anxiety are common in demanding courses and are treatable.

parts.why: Problems are smaller and easier to treat when caught early, the same way a small leak is easier to fix than a flood. Young people often delay asking because of embarrassment, worry about what others will think, or not knowing that what they feel counts as "bad enough". Knowing in advance where to go removes one of those barriers. You do not have to be in crisis to deserve support.
parts.how:
1. Find out now, while you are well, what your school, university or employer offers: counselling, wellbeing staff, disability or learning support, a tutor or mentor.
  2. Book an appointment with a doctor (GP) if low mood, anxiety, sleep problems or exhaustion last more than two weeks or affect daily life.
  3. Tell one trusted person (a friend, family member or tutor) how you are really doing.
  4. If you are in immediate danger or think you might harm yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line in your country straight away.

examples.simple: A first-year student who keeps waking at 4 am worrying about exams goes to the university counselling service and gets a few sessions plus practical tools.
examples.nontrivial: A mature student with a job and children feels constantly behind and assumes it is just a time-management problem. Talking to a disability adviser reveals possible ADHD; an assessment and adjustments (extra exam time, recorded lectures) change the picture more than any planner could.
